say.text: A 48-year-old man had short bouts of right upper pain after fatty meals, each settling within 3 hours.
This time the pain has lasted 30 hours. Temperature 38.2 °C, right upper abdomen tender, Murphy's sign positive.
What is your working diagnosis?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: In acute cholecystitis, a blockage starts the inflammation. Which blockage most often does?

choices.label: A stone stuck in the cystic duct or Hartmann's pouch
A stone stuck in the common bile duct
Infected bile with no stone at all
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The same stone can cause biliary colic or acute cholecystitis.
What differs at the gallbladder itself?

choices.label: Outlet blocked only briefly, wall not inflamed
Colicky spasm in waves, however long it lasts
Stone permanently fixed in the common duct
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Under the Tokyo Guidelines 2018 (TG18), which combination makes a suspected diagnosis of acute cholecystitis?

choices.label: One local sign plus one systemic sign
One local sign, one systemic sign and imaging
Ultrasound stones plus one local sign
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: A 52-year-old man: Murphy's sign is positive and his temperature is 38.5 °C. Ultrasound has not been done yet.
Which TG18 level fits him now?

choices.label: Suspected: local and systemic signs both present
Definite: the bedside signs already prove it
Not diagnosable until imaging is done
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The same patient now has an ultrasound report showing the imaging findings of acute cholecystitis.
Which TG18 level is he at now?

choices.label: Definite: all three sets are now met
Suspected: imaging does not change the level
Definite: the two bedside sets are enough
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: A 66-year-old man has painless jaundice. His gallbladder is palpable and non-tender.
What does Courvoisier's law suggest here?

choices.label: Malignant distal obstruction, so not gallstones
Any palpable gallbladder means cancer, jaundice or not
A palpable gallbladder excludes gallstone disease here
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: A 40-year-old woman has fever and a tender right upper mass. She is not jaundiced.
Does Courvoisier's law apply?

choices.label: No: the law needs jaundice, so it does not apply
Yes: any palpable gallbladder is malignant until proven otherwise
Yes, but only if the mass is not tender
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Which of these is Courvoisier's law?

choices.label: With jaundice, a non-tender palpable gallbladder is unlikely to be stones
Any palpable gallbladder, jaundiced or not, suggests malignancy
A tender palpable gallbladder with fever suggests carcinoma of the gallbladder
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Pain beyond about 6 hours, with fever and local tenderness, points to **acute cholecystitis**.
Murphy's sign is catching of breath on deep palpation under the right ribs. You will need that local sign again.
That is not the right choice.
Colic is tempting: fatty meals and shoulder pain fit it, and it is the first name you learn for stone pain. But colic is steady and settles within hours, so the clock here points away from it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the clock first: duration and fever come before the name of the pain.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
A bile-duct stone is tempting, since a stone with fever feels like a duct problem. But no jaundice is described, and the inflammation sits in the gallbladder wall.

sure_note.text: You were sure: a stone nearby does not move the disease to the duct. Ask where the inflammation sits.

say.text: Two clues decide it: how many hours the pain has lasted, and whether the gallbladder wall is inflamed. Check the fever and the tenderness, then choose again.
Yes. Most acute cholecystitis is calculous, in about 90–95% of cases, with the stone impacted in the cystic duct or Hartmann's pouch.
That is not the right choice.
A duct stone is tempting, since common bile duct stones are the ones that cause jaundice and worry. But they cause duct disease, and this inflammation starts at the gallbladder's own outlet.
That is not the right choice.
Acalculous disease is tempting, since infected bile with no stone sounds like the same illness. But it is the minority; most cases start with a stone blocking the outlet, and infection follows.
Ask what blocks the gallbladder first, then where that stone sits. Choose again.
Right. Colic is a brief outlet block with a normal wall. Cholecystitis keeps the block and inflames the wall.
That is not the right choice.

Colic is tempting, since everyone calls stone pain colic and pictures cramping in waves. But colic is steady rather than wavy, and the word says nothing about duration: pain past 6 hours with fever is inflammation.
That is not the right choice.
A stone fixed in the common duct is tempting, since it sounds like the most serious version. But that is a duct stone, and this question is about what happens at the gallbladder.
Ask two things: how long the outlet stays blocked, and whether the wall becomes inflamed. Choose again.
Yes. Suspected uses the bedside sets only: one local sign and one systemic sign. Imaging is added at the definite level.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Rebuild the sets: suspected uses bedside signs only, and imaging is added to reach definite.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Stones on ultrasound look like the whole diagnosis, so they feel like enough. But they belong to the imaging set, and the suspected level is built from clinical signs first.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Stones are an imaging finding, so they cannot stand in for a clinical sign.

say.text: Split the findings into local signs, systemic signs and imaging. Which sets does the suspected rule use? Choose again.
Yes. Murphy's sign is a local sign and fever is a systemic one, so he meets the suspected level.
Definite waits for the imaging set.
That is not the right choice.
Signs this clear feel like proof, so calling the case definite is tempting. But definite also needs the imaging set, and no scan has been done yet.

Count the findings in each set: local signs, systemic signs and imaging. Which sets are already met? Choose again.
Yes. Definite is the bedside sets plus the imaging set. The characteristic imaging finding is what upgrades a suspected case.
That is not the right choice.
A scan can seem like a supporting extra, so keeping the level unchanged feels safe. But the imaging set is one of the three, and a characteristic scan moves suspected to definite.

Yes. In jaundice, a palpable non-tender gallbladder is unlikely to be stones and suggests malignant distal obstruction, such as carcinoma of the pancreatic head.

The law is often memorised as a one-line cancer sign, so any palpable gallbladder feels malignant. But the law is about jaundiced patients, and this patient is jaundiced.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the qualifiers first: jaundice, then tenderness, then the sign.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
A palpable mass seems to settle the question, since the mass explains the picture. But the law says stones are unlikely, not excluded, and it is about jaundice.

sure_note.text: You were sure. The law lowers the odds of stones; it does not rule them out.

say.text: Check the two qualifiers in order: is the patient jaundiced, and is the gallbladder tender? Choose again.
Yes. The law's qualifier is jaundice. A tender mass with fever suggests empyema or mucocele, which does not contradict the law.
That is not the right choice.
A palpable gallbladder feels like a cancer clue, and the law is remembered that way. But the law is about a jaundiced patient, and this woman has no jaundice.
That is not the right choice.
Tenderness is tempting as the feature that sets this mass apart. But the law's qualifier is jaundice, not tenderness, and a tender mass with fever points to inflammation.

Yes. The law needs jaundice and a non-tender gallbladder, and points to malignant distal obstruction rather than stones.
That is not the right choice.
The short form of the law sounds like a cancer rule for any lump. But the statement hinges on jaundice, and a palpable gallbladder without it is not the law's case.
That is not the right choice.
Carcinoma is the feared cause, so a tender mass with fever feels like it belongs to the law. But tenderness with fever is inflammation, and the law is about a non-tender mass in jaundice.
